dialogue.text: Last week the flour cost me nine hundred Egyptian pounds a sack. Today it's eleven hundred. My customers think I'm the one getting rich.

[serious, engaging] In 2011, rising food prices helped push Egyptians into the streets, and eighteen days later their president was gone. In America, the crash arrives a different way: as a calendar invite.

[serious, engaging] Week three. In Shanghai, China's factories can make almost anything, but the people who buy their stuff just watched their savings shrink, so they stop ordering. The world's busiest port goes quiet.
Eighteen days at anchor. Full fuel tank, empty containers, and my crew has started a card tournament.

[serious, engaging] Fewer ships means fewer trucks and fewer warehouses. In Ohio, the warehouse that unloads those containers cuts its whole night shift. In the last big crash, America lost almost nine million jobs, and for a lot of people it started with a fifteen-minute meeting called quick sync.
Thanks for jumping on. This won't take long.
[serious, engaging] And in month two, people start asking the question nobody wants to ask out loud: is my money in the bank even safe?
